concept: Zone sharding for tiered hardware (hot, warm, cold)
summary: Source-anchored research for Zone sharding for tiered hardware (hot, warm, cold). Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Zone names are chosen by the operator; MongoDB's tiered-hardware tutorial uses two hardware-based zones named "recent" (fast tier) and "archive" (archival tier), and zones are generally usable to route data by the hardware/performance of shards. Hot, warm and cold are not fixed MongoDB storage classes. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/sharding-tiered-hardware-for-varying-slas.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/zone-sharding.md

Rolling retention tiers require an operator or automation to update absolute date boundaries. The balancer enforces the configured ranges; a fixed boundary does not advance merely because documents become older. Rotation frequency trades operational frequency against migration volume per rotation. (medium confidence)

To benefit from targeted reads, queries should include the relevant shard key or usable prefix. Queries without it can broadcast across shards, so a cold tier can remain part of an application read path even when most user-facing data is recent. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/sharded-cluster-query-router.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/sharding-tiered-hardware-for-varying-slas.md

Configure zone placement before allowing newly added low-spec shards to receive ordinary balancing traffic. Percona warns that adding those shards with the balancer running can move unintended data; MongoDB's hardware-tier tutorial stops balancing while configuring zones. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.percona.com/blog/tactics-to-scale-down-your-mongodb-deployment/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/sharding-tiered-hardware-for-varying-slas.md

A reported hot/cold configuration with shard key order {id, ts} used MinKey-to-MaxKey spans for id in both ranges and failed with an overlapping-zone-range error. This illustrates why a trailing timestamp cannot be treated as an independent age partition across every leading id. (medium confidence)

Zone configuration needs eligible destination shards. The balancer migrates a chunk whose range falls into a zone only into a shard inside that zone, and the tiered-hardware tutorial requires adding each shard to a zone, so a tier label and its date ranges alone do not provision working cold capacity. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/zone-sharding.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/sharding-tiered-hardware-for-varying-slas.md

Age-based placement needs a shard key whose ordered ranges can distinguish the ages being separated. A creation-date prefix can support this; hashing the age field makes its zone ranges operate on hash values rather than chronological intervals. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/sharding-tiered-hardware-for-varying-slas.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/zone-sharding.md ; https://www.percona.com/blog/tactics-to-scale-down-your-mongodb-deployment/

Zone ranges include their lower bound and exclude their upper bound, and zones cannot share or overlap ranges. MaxKey compares higher than every other value and MinKey lower, so a range whose upper bound uses MaxKey and one whose lower bound uses MinKey do not meet at the same boundary; in the tiered-hardware tutorial the archive range's upper bound is set to the same value as the recent range's lower bound. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/zone-sharding.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/bson-type-comparison-order.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/sharding-tiered-hardware-for-varying-slas.md

Zone sharding maps shard-key ranges to named groups of shards. Assigning recent and archival ranges to shards with different hardware lets one collection serve data with different latency requirements. (high confidence)

Cold-shard economics depend on having a significant fraction of cold data that can tolerate slower latency on the few occasions it is accessed. Cheaper shards (smaller RAM and CPU, higher-latency/lower-throughput disks) can reduce cost, and the archive tier in MongoDB's tutorial uses less RAM, slower disks and more basic CPUs with more storage per server. Percona claims disk savings can exceed 50% once you have terabytes of disk, but this is one author's estimate, not a generally applicable figure. Sources: https://www.percona.com/blog/tactics-to-scale-down-your-mongodb-deployment/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/sharding-tiered-hardware-for-varying-slas.md

Zone changes converge through chunk migrations. Existing chunks can violate the new placement rules until balancing completes, and migration activity can affect cluster performance; plan rotation timing and verify final placement. (high confidence)
Ranges outside all configured zones may reside on any shard. Cover the intended chronological domain explicitly if hot/warm/cold hardware placement must apply to all records. (high confidence)

A monotonically increasing timestamp used for range sharding can concentrate new writes on the highest-key chunk and its shard. Hardware tiering therefore does not by itself distribute concurrent new inserts across the hot shards. (high confidence)
